newsitem.title: USA: U.S., N.Korea fail to bridge peace talks gap.
newsitem.headline: U.S., N.Korea fail to bridge peace talks gap.

text.p: North Korea and the United States failed to make significant headway toward holding four-nation peace talks at their latest meeting, U.S. officials said on Friday.
Contrary to a Washington-datelined report from Japan's Kyodo News Agency on Thursday, the officials said Pyongyang had presented no potential breakthrough ideas.
"They were not running around with new ideas" at the meeting on Thursday in New York between working-level officials, one said, adding: "No breakthroughs at this one."

Kyodo cited an unnamed source as saying North Korea had made a new proposal on the proposed quadrilateral talks that the United States deemed worth considering. But officials said the Kyodo report was off-base.

The United States used the session largely to press North Korea to free Carl Hunziker, a U.S. citizen held since Aug. 24 on spying charges, but North Korea had shown no inclination to do so, one official said.

On Thursday, State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns ruled out an apology to Pyongyang over Hunziker and ridiculed North Korean charges that his alleged religious ignorance proved he was not a missionary but a spy.
"They think he's a useful political tool," an official familiar with the New York meeting said, adding that such a view showed a complete misunderstanding of the United States.

He said resolving the deadlock over Hunziker, described by family members as a 26-year-old missionary, was important to clear the way for progress on other pending issues, notably the proposed peace talks.

The United States and South Korea jointly proposed the four-nation talks in April, inviting North Korea and China to join in a dialogue aimed at replacing the truce that ended the 1950-53 Korean War with a lasting peace for the Korean peninsula. North Korea has not yet agreed to take part.
Another working-level U.S.-North Korean meeting could take place next week, a U.S. official said. Another official predicted "more tough slogging."
The State Department is concerned that Communist North Korea may be preparing to test-fire a missile capable of reaching Japan, adding to tensions in Northeast Asia.

Taking part in Thursday's meeting were were Ri Hyong Chol, director of the North Korean Foreign Ministry's American Affairs Bureau, and Mark Minton, director of the State Department's Korean Affairs Office.
